title: Pakistan's System Has Collapsed, Says Interior Minister Naqvi, Fueling Coup Speculation
excerpt: Speaking at the Pakistan Economic Summit, Mohsin Naqvi — Army Chief Asim Munir's closest political ally — warned that frustrated youth could "overturn everything," drawing comparisons to India's Cockroach Janta Party movement. The army distanced itself from his remarks.
body:
• Pakistan Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi declared the governance system has "collapsed" at the Pakistan Economic Summit in Islamabad
  • Naqvi warned that frustrated youth — whom he called "cockroaches" — could "overturn everything" if the system is not fixed
  • The Pakistan Army distanced itself from Naqvi's remarks, with ISPR DG calling them his "personal opinion"
  • The speech has fueled speculation about whether Pakistan's hybrid civilian-military regime is preparing the ground for direct military rule

Pakistan's Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi has triggered a political firestorm by declaring that the country's governance system has "collapsed" and warning that angry youth could overthrow the existing order.

Speaking at the Pakistan Economic Summit in Islamabad, Naqvi — widely regarded as the closest political ally of Army Chief Field Marshal Asim Munir — called for a complete reset of Pakistan's administrative structure. His remarks have revived speculation about whether the country's hybrid civilian-military regime is laying the groundwork for more direct military intervention.

The "Cockroaches" Warning

In the most incendiary portion of his speech, Naqvi used the term "cockroaches" to describe Pakistan's frustrated young population — borrowing symbolism from India's Cockroach Janta Party, a student movement that gained traction after a remark by India's Chief Justice Surya Kant and eventually forced the country's education minister to resign.

"We are unable to give our youth what they want. Call them youngsters, call them cockroaches, or whatever you like. But if these cockroaches come together, they can overturn everything."

— Mohsin Naqvi, Interior Minister of Pakistan

Naqvi said Pakistan's youth are demanding a fair system, justice, merit-based opportunities, and employment — not government handouts like stipend programs or free tablets. He warned that if young people unite around their shared grievances, they could transform the country's political landscape.

A social media campaign calling itself "Cockroach Party Pakistan" has gained over 114,000 followers on Instagram, describing itself as a youth-led movement fighting corruption and poor governance with the slogan: "Pakistan belongs to its people, not corrupt mafias."

Army Distances Itself

Naqvi's comments were raised during a press briefing with ISPR Director General Lt Gen Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry. Asked whether the army agreed that Pakistan's governance system had failed, Chaudhry declined to endorse the remarks.

"The interior minister's comments are his personal opinion. I will not comment on them," Chaudhry said. He added that good governance was only possible in a "secure and stable Pakistan" and that it was for political parties to decide how such governance should be achieved.

The army's careful distancing is notable given Naqvi's close ties to the military establishment. As both Interior Minister and chairman of the Pakistan Cricket Board, Naqvi occupies an unusually powerful position in Pakistan's civilian government and is widely seen as Munir's political proxy.

Calls for System Reset

Naqvi argued that Pakistan's financial problems reflect deeper structural failures. The federal government, he said, begins every budget with a deficit and focuses only on borrowing more money each year. No matter how hard the prime minister works, meaningful change is impossible unless the governance system is fundamentally reset, he said.

He proposed creating more administrative units to improve public service delivery and create space for new political leadership. The Pakistan Peoples Party's Nayyar Bukhari pushed back, noting that any proposal to create new provinces must follow Pakistan's constitutional process, requiring approval from the concerned provincial assembly and a two-thirds majority in both houses of Parliament.

Coup History Casts a Long Shadow

Pakistan's military has a long history of asserting dominance over civilian governments, staging coups in 1958, 1977, and most recently in 1999 when General Pervez Musharraf toppled then-Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif — the brother of the current premier, Shehbaz Sharif.

Former President Arif Alvi, responding to Naqvi's remarks on X, argued that the system itself had not failed — rather, those controlling it had destroyed it. Alvi alleged that electoral manipulation had weakened parliamentary democracy and that the imprisonment of former Prime Minister Imran Khan had further damaged democratic institutions.

The current political setup is often described as a hybrid model. Defence Minister Khawaja Asif has previously acknowledged it is "not an ideal democratic government" while insisting it functions "very well." Army Chief Munir's solo meeting with President Trump earlier this year — conducted without Prime Minister Sharif or the foreign minister present — underscored the military's outsized role in civilian affairs.
nri_angle: Pakistan's deepening governance crisis and coup speculation carry direct implications for India-Pakistan relations, regional stability, and the broader South Asian diaspora community.
author: Diaspora Desk
